title: Gradient descent vs BFGS vs Newton
sub: Lines are the paths each method takes over the contour map. Green dot: the minimum.

frames.caption: A tilted, narrow bowl (12 times steeper one way than the other). All three start at the same point and use exact line searches.
Step 1. Newton uses the true curvature and lands on the minimum in one step. BFGS knows nothing yet, so its first step is plain gradient descent.
Step 2. BFGS has learned the curvature from one gradient difference and finishes: 2 steps in 2 dimensions, as the theory promises for quadratics.
Step 3. Gradient descent zigzags across the valley: each step heads straight downhill, which points mostly at the valley wall.
Step 4. Gradient descent zigzags across the valley: each step heads straight downhill, which points mostly at the valley wall.
Step 5. Gradient descent zigzags across the valley: each step heads straight downhill, which points mostly at the valley wall.
Step 6. Gradient descent zigzags across the valley: each step heads straight downhill, which points mostly at the valley wall.
Step 7. Gradient descent zigzags across the valley: each step heads straight downhill, which points mostly at the valley wall.
Gradient descent needs 46 steps to get within 0.0001, and the narrower the bowl, the worse it gets. BFGS needed 2, Newton 1.

Rosenbrock's banana: a curved, flat-bottomed valley with the minimum at (1, 1), a classic stress test. Same start for all three. Gradient descent uses the largest fixed step that doesn't blow up; the other two use a line search.
Step 3. BFGS and Newton drop into the valley at once. The hard part is following its curve to the minimum.
Step 12. Newton, with the exact Hessian, is racing along the valley floor. BFGS is learning the curvature as it goes.
Step 25. Gradient descent is stuck crawling in the valley: the floor is so flat that the gradient barely points along it.
To get within 0.0001 of the minimum: Newton 20 steps, BFGS 32 steps, gradient descent 19,034 steps. BFGS gets most of Newton's speed without ever computing a Hessian.
